title: Army Cyber Command wants agents that neutralise targets themselves
summary: The Intercept reports that US Army Cyber Command is developing a platform codenamed ECHOTRIBBLE to turn AI agents into autonomous cyberweapons. An ARCYBER document circulated to potential contractors describes agents "designed to autonomously navigate infrastructures" and capable of "identifying and neutralizing identified threats/targets", and says the software "must operate with minimal human oversight" and must be capable of "Self-Directed Behavior". A Q&A document for vendors says the programme is "primarily focused" on offensive missions, and that neutralising a target could include "disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target". ARCYBER did not respond to The Intercept's questions.

Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, subject to stockholder approval, with the board adding at its discretion a further 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a baseline CNBC says has yet to be disclosed. CNBC reports Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of an IPO reportedly slated for November. Separately, Meta says an automated security system wrongly suspended the Instagram account of the No Kings Coalition during a weekend of nationwide demonstrations, and blames a tool from Anthropic's Claude that it says was reading profiles, posts and hashtags at roughly four times the normal rate.

Kyiv Post, relaying a Bloomberg review, says the Russian-linked network tracked as Matryoshka circulated 130 fabricated videos and doctored newspaper front pages between 10 September and 9 October, attacking Democratic candidates in 20 of the 35 US Senate races and 29 of the 36 gubernatorial contests on the 3 November ballot. And an audit of 33,000 agent trajectories finds most prompt injections that fail against small tool-using agents are silently ignored rather than refused, with attack success on InjecAgent moving from 0.2% to 43% when only the system prompt changed.

items.headline: Anthropic commits 5% of its shares to a wholly owned public benefit fund, subject to stockholder approval
bullets: Anthropic's post says 5% of its shares will be committed to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, subject to stockholder approval, with the board adding at its discretion an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline. CNBC says that baseline "has yet to be disclosed".

Anthropic says the fund will be a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit, to allow adjustability between different forms of giving, and that equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the US or internationally. Anthropic says the money could go to large donations to traditional nonprofits or to direct distributions to specific populations.

Anthropic says co-founder pledges and an employee equity donation match already bring roughly 20% of its shares to the public good before any valuation-milestone additions, and that it has already committed $200 million to studying AI's labour-market effects.

CNBC reports Anthropic told investors third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of an IPO reportedly slated for November, and quotes Lise Buyer of IPO advisory firm Class V Group saying the timing is "both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and 'beneficial from an image perspective'". Anthropic has not said who will decide what the fund pays for; it says structure, governance and valuation milestones will be shared "in the coming months".

items.headline: Audit of 33,000 agent trajectories finds 76-80% of failed prompt injections were ignored, not refused
bullets: The paper audits "33,000 trajectories from eleven open-weight agents (2-14B parameters)" on InjecAgent and AgentDojo, and reports that a label-blind LLM judge "shows that most failed attacks are ignored (76-80%) rather than refused (17-18%)".

It reports that "with identical model weights, changing only the system prompt shifts InjecAgent ASR from 0.2% to 43%" — so a low attack success rate can be a property of the scaffolding rather than of the model.

Its Attack-Task Outcome Matrix reports that in 21.7% of AgentDojo episodes "the agent stayed safe but did not complete the user's task", which attack-success-rate scoring counts as a successful defence. The authors argue evaluations should report how attacks fail and whether the user's task was completed, alongside ASR.

The paper is a preprint by Farhan Zarif and six co-authors; neither the arXiv abstract page nor the HTML title page lists author affiliations, and the results cover open-weight models of 2-14B parameters, not frontier systems.

items.headline: Automated repository poisoning of coding agents reports over 60% poisoning success across 384 repositories
bullets: The paper presents TrojanForge, which parses a repository into abstract syntax trees, uses a security review agent to pick the least conspicuous injection point, and iteratively refines its disguise by adversarial play against the target agent. The abstract opens: "Coding agents are increasingly capable with autonomy, which exposes them to repository-level poisoning."

It introduces TrojanBench, a benchmark of 384 poisoned repositories spanning 6 domains and 9 programming languages, and reports a stable poisoning success rate above 60% and a backdoor injection rate exceeding 90% across 4 harnesses and 12 models.

The authors state that even commercial agents fail to defend against repository-level poisoning. The paper describes attacks on agents that read untrusted repositories, not a compromise of any named product.

The paper is a preprint by Xiao Yang and five co-authors; the HTML title page gives affiliations including Baidu Inc. and Beihang University in Beijing and East China Normal University in Shanghai. No independent replication exists.

items.headline: SenseNova-led evaluation puts GPT-6-Astra at 81.9% on RoboDojo in simulation but 0 of 11 real plug insertions
bullets: The report evaluates GPT-6-Astra across "12 representative benchmarks" covering tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms and dexterous hands, and its introduction states the model achieves "81.9% on RoboDojo and 87.3% on DexJoCo". On the LIBERO series, section 2.4 says "success at the standard budget already exceeds 97%".

Real-world testing on 8 robot configurations reports a different picture: "rigid pick-and-place is reliable (17/18 trials)", but "cloth folding: 2/4 on the Franka 3" and "plug insertion: 0/11 across three platforms". The abstract says the experiments "reveal substantial gaps".

The authors conclude the model has largely reached embodied competence but not practical embodied intelligence — a gap between benchmark scores and contact-rich physical tasks that the benchmarks do not capture.

The paper is a preprint credited to "SenseNova and Joint Research Team" with 60 named authors; the HTML title page lists no institutions. The evaluation was run by the authors on a model they do not make, and no independent replication exists.

items.headline: Reward models fine-tuned to prefer harm in one domain generalised to seven held-out domains
bullets: The paper reports fine-tuning two Skywork-Reward-V2 reward models — the Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B variants — to prefer harmful responses in a single domain, either medical or financial, and that the preference generalised to seven held-out domains.
It reports overall losses of 4.8 and 5.3 points on RewardBench 2 for the fine-tuned models, meaning a reward model can be corrupted while still scoring close to normal on a standard benchmark.

The paper traces the mechanism to the last scored token in two steps: safe and harmful representations are first compressed so the angle between them shrinks, then harmful representations rotate closer to the scalar reward head.

The paper is a preprint by Dhruv Puri and Nikhil Prakash of Northeastern University. The abstract's wording leaves it ambiguous which of the two point drops belongs to which model, and the work covers 8B open-weight reward models rather than those used at frontier labs.

items.headline: Claude Opus 5.5 explained half the variance in ML experiment outcomes across 288 proposed ideas
bullets: The paper built a dataset of 288 LLM-proposed ideas across eight MLE-bench tasks, implemented and scored each one, then asked five frontier models — GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3 — to predict each idea's effect before training.

It reports the best of them, Claude Opus 5.5, reached R² = 0.49 and "explains only half of the variance in outcomes", and that "all tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of the changes".
The result bears on automated research agents, which rely on a model's judgement about which experiment to run before spending compute on it.

The paper is a preprint by Ayush Bansal and four co-authors; no institutions are listed on the arXiv abstract page. The abstract does not give R² values for the other four models, and the authors note each idea was run only once, so training noise is unquantified.

items.headline: Bloomberg review: Russian-linked Matryoshka network aimed 130 fabricated videos at US midterm candidates
bullets: Kyiv Post, relaying a Bloomberg News review, says Bloomberg examined 130 fabricated videos and doctored newspaper front pages circulated between 10 September and 9 October 2026 and attributed to the network tracked as Matryoshka, also called Operation Overload. Kyiv Post describes the campaign as "focused almost exclusively on Democratic contenders".

The material targeted Democratic candidates in 20 of the 35 US Senate races and 29 of the 36 gubernatorial contests on the 3 November ballot, naming Texas Senate nominee James Talarico and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff. Talarico's spokesperson denied the claim made against him, and Kyiv Post says no public records substantiate the claim about Ossoff.

The clips use synthetic likenesses of Robert De Niro, Julia Roberts and Cher, and impersonate ABC News and CBS News broadcasts. Antibot4Navalny, which monitors Kremlin-aligned networks, says views "can jump as high as 200,000 within the first hour but then quickly plateau", a pattern Kyiv Post attributes to bot networks manipulating view counts.

Kyiv Post says the US open-source intelligence firms Graphika and dTeam corroborated the findings. The underlying Bloomberg investigation published before this window and bloomberg.com could not be opened from here; the figures above are quoted as Kyiv Post relays them.

items.headline: Zimbabwe police begin texting fines for 4.8 million offences recorded by Harare's AI cameras
bullets: The Zimbabwe Republic Police announced on Saturday that its Smart Traffic Management System is "now fully functional and operational in selected Central Business Districts (CBDs) across the country", and zimDaily reports police have begun sending SMS notices for 4.8 million offences recorded by AI cameras, each with a video clip and the fine attached. zimDaily says the 4.8 million figure was in The Herald by Sunday morning.

The count has climbed fast: Home Affairs permanent secretary Raphael Faranisi put it at about 1.1 million vehicles flagged in early August and 2.3 million by mid-August, and police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi said it had passed four million late in September. The standard Level 3 penalty is US$30 payable in ZiG, with speeding tiered at US$5 for six to 15 km/h over the limit, US$15 for 16 to 25 over and US$30 for 26 to 50 over. Phase One covers 20 junctions; the full plan covers 326 intersections in four phases.

The cameras do more than read plates. When Cabinet approved the system in June 2025, Information Minister Jenfan Muswere said it included "intelligent cameras with Automatic Number Plate and Face Recognition, AI-powered video analytics" and that the network could "detect and monitor incidents such as crowd gatherings, loitering, and pickpocketing". ZRP Commissioner Evelyn Taurai Phillip later listed the national identity database among the systems being plugged into it.

zimDaily reports the City of Harare admitted in May last year that 21 of the 69 signal-controlled junctions in the central business district were not working, that Faranisi conceded some recorded violations may have occurred while an officer was directing traffic by hand, and that it could find no published procedure for how a disputed clip will be reviewed. Courteney Mukoyi of the Justice Court Foundation is quoted warning that "using nationwide facial recognition to monitor people's movements may then be disproportionate". Only one outlet carries the 4.8 million SMS rollout.

items.headline: OpenCode co-founder says attackers probed its systems non-stop for 48 hours after the API-key breach
bullets: The Hacker News reports that on 18 October OpenCode co-founder Dax Raad said on X that attackers had been "non stop trying to attack our systems for the past 48 hours", and that "a side effect is everything is getting hardened". That is the only dated development since the disclosure covered in yesterday's edition.

On the earlier facts: an intruder reached a legacy system on the night of 16 October, OpenCode says 1.4% of Console users were affected — all of whom had an outside AI provider linked — and affected users were emailed on the morning of 17 October. Raad said provider keys added through the command-line and desktop apps sit in a local SQLite database and "never come to us".

Users reported unauthorised charges ranging from about $168 to $1,700, including one report of $281 in OpenAI charges and $168 in Anthropic charges, another of $1,700 in total, a Reddit report of $400 on Anthropic, and about €200 in Google usage before the project was suspended.

The Hacker News lists what OpenCode has not explained: how the breach connects to the "large-scale distillation attack" its 17 October post referred to, what the legacy system was, how many keys it held, what 1.4% of users is in absolute numbers, when the unauthorised access began, and whether any key was actually copied or used — the company has said only that keys "may have been exposed".

items.headline: Odisha opposition party files police complaint over AI voice-cloned videos of former bureaucrat
bullets: BJD leader Amrita Mishra filed a complaint at Capital police station in Bhubaneswar against the unidentified operators of the Instagram and Facebook account "Odianka Chhata", over videos the party says were made with AI and voice cloning to target former bureaucrat and BJD leader Sujata Rout Karthikeyan.

The complaint says videos uploaded on 18 October allegedly show her phoning the principal of Kendrapara Autonomous College, threatening him and trying to influence student union elections, and states that "the said content is entirely fabricated and has been manufactured with the sole intent to mislead the public".

The complaint asks police to register an FIR, preserve digital evidence, conduct a forensic examination of the material, obtain information from Meta through lawful channels and stop further circulation. Odisha Bytes says police confirmed they are investigating, and that the account reportedly began posting AI-generated videos after student union elections held across Odisha on 15 October.

Odisha Bytes does not independently confirm that the videos are synthetic and reports no forensic finding, police conclusion or identification of who runs the account. The fabrication claim is the complainant's.

items.headline: Army Cyber Command is building ECHOTRIBBLE, AI agents meant to neutralise targets with minimal human oversight
bullets: The Intercept, citing an ARCYBER document circulated to potential contractors, reports that US Army Cyber Command is developing a platform codenamed ECHOTRIBBLE to turn AI agents into autonomous cyberweapons. The document describes agents "designed to autonomously navigate infrastructures" and capable of "identifying and neutralizing identified threats/targets", says the software "must operate with minimal human oversight", and requires it to be capable of "Self-Directed Behavior".

A Q&A document for potential contractors says ECHOTRIBBLE is "primarily focused" on offensive missions, and that neutralising a target could include "disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target".

A PowerPoint presented to vendors at a 24 June ARCYBER event gives a hypothetical in which the software, once uploaded to a laptop, independently finds other potential targets on the same network and then produces a replica of itself tailored for an iPad, an Apple desktop and a Windows 11 PC — self-propagation decided by the agent rather than an operator.

David Krueger, a machine learning professor at the University of Montreal and founder of Evitable, told The Intercept that "making autonomous AI systems with a mandate to 'neutralize threats' is incredibly dangerous". Hyrum Anderson, co-founder and chief executive of the AI security firm Abundant, asked: "The target may well be hit. But what path will it take?" ARCYBER did not respond to The Intercept's questions, including about measures to prevent inadvertent damage. The documents describe a programme in development; no deployment or contract award is reported.

items.headline: Tech Policy Press names the courts for all eight state suits against OpenAI and four new private cases
bullets: Tim Bernard and Justin Hendrix name the court for each of the eight state attorney general suits filed on 14 October 2026: Maricopa County Superior Court (Arizona), Faulkner County Circuit Court (Arkansas), Ada County District Court (Idaho), Polk County District Court (Iowa), Shawnee County District Court (Kansas), Lewis and Clark County District Court (Montana), Buffalo County District Court (Nebraska) and Mason County Circuit Court (West Virginia). With Florida, which sued in June, the article says the claims will be considered "in parallel in nine different state courts".

It reports that Arkansas's complaint asks the court to "Enjoin Defendants from creating models capable of recursive self-improvement" until they can ensure such models "will be aligned with human values" — a request to bar a capability rather than a product.

It identifies a proposed class action, Doe v. OpenAI, filed 13 October 2026 in the US District Court for the Northern District of California for a mother, her 12-year-old daughter and her 16-year-old son. It cites Section 1568.5 of California's Civil Code and seeks a declaration voiding OpenAI's terms under an 1874 California rule limiting minors' contracts, plus an unjust enrichment claim.

Four suits filed on 14 October 2026 in San Francisco Superior Court by Tech Justice Law are named — Gates v. OpenAI, Works v. OpenAI, Hill v. OpenAI and Habib v. OpenAI — and are expected to join Judicial Council Coordination Proceeding No. 5431. OpenAI told NBC it has "built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack"; the article says OpenAI has not publicly addressed the Tech Justice Law suits.

items.headline: Nvidia asks Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to build NVHBM base dies on TSMC's 3-nanometer process
bullets: Seoul Economic Daily reports Nvidia wants the base die of its custom NVHBM memory — the logic layer carrying the memory controller that previously sat on the GPU — made on TSMC's 3-nanometer logic process, and that Samsung is working with TSMC on it at Nvidia's request. Electronics Weekly, citing the same paper, reports Samsung and Micron "have agreed to Nvidia's request" with "volume production expected in 2027".

The paper puts industry estimates of TSMC's 3nm yield above 90%, against roughly 60% for Samsung Foundry's 2nm SF2 process, and says Samsung's own 4-nanometer base die lines are limited to Hwaseong Line 17 and part of Pyeongtaek P3, so it cannot easily absorb custom HBM volumes. Samsung is validating NVHBM base die production on its 2nm process as a hedge.

Electronics Weekly says Nvidia wants one common base die design and process across suppliers so it does not have to validate each vendor's version separately, and notes SK hynix was already using TSMC's 12nm process for HBM4 base dies. Nvidia's claimed gains for NVHBM over standard HBM4E are up to 30% more bandwidth and 15% lower power.

Both accounts trace to one Korean newspaper citing unnamed industry sources, and the Seoul Economic Daily article itself carries no bandwidth or power figures. Order volumes, supply ratios and mass-production timelines are undisclosed, and none of Nvidia, Samsung, SK hynix, Micron or TSMC has confirmed the arrangement.

items.headline: Some Nscale backers want a $16bn to $19bn IPO valuation against the company's roughly $30bn goal
bullets: PYMNTS, citing a Bloomberg News report published 18 October 2026 that relied on people familiar with the matter, says "some backers are balking at the company's initial public offering (IPO) goal of around $30 billion" and want $16 billion to $19 billion instead.

Nscale filed to go public on 18 September and the required 15-day waiting period has passed, but formal marketing has not begun and the company is still responding to SEC comments, with no decisions made.

PYMNTS says investors are weighing Microsoft's withdrawal from its Nscale data centre agreement, which Microsoft attributed to delays tied to power constraints, and the collapse of Australian data centre firm Firmus's IPO plans. Nscale committed at least $3.5 billion, and up to $6 billion, to support Figure's AI models and robots under a multi-year deal signed last month.

This updates the Microsoft Loughton exit reported in yesterday's edition. The valuation figures come from PYMNTS' account of the Bloomberg report, as bloomberg.com returned a bot-check page and could not be opened. Nscale has not publicly commented on the range.

items.headline: Samsung Electro-Mechanics wins a 360.5 billion won memory-substrate contract from an undisclosed customer
bullets: Seoul Economic Daily reports a contract worth 360.5 billion won, about $251 million, for package substrates for memory chips, running one year from 1 January to 31 December 2027. The customer is described only as "a global big tech company" whose name was withheld under a confidentiality agreement.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics said the contract equals 3.2% of its consolidated revenue from last year, and the paper says it is the company's seventh long-term supply contract since May, bringing the total to 4.3 trillion won.
The paper attributes the demand to high-performance memory for AI servers, including DRAM and HBM, which it says requires densely packed multilayer fine circuits that minimise signal loss.
The customer is not named, so the link to any specific AI programme is the paper's inference from the product type rather than a disclosed fact. Only one outlet carries it.

items.headline: Meta says a Claude tool browsing at four times the normal rate triggered the No Kings Instagram suspension
bullets: Andy Stone, Meta's vice president of communications, wrote in a social media post on Sunday that Instagram's engineering team found a tool from Anthropic PBC's Claude was accessing profiles, posts and hashtags "at roughly four times the normal rate in intense bursts Saturday", and that "these abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems".

The No Kings Coalition said its Instagram page was unavailable for about 90 minutes, with full access restored at 5:33 p.m. New York time on Saturday; Meta says an automated review about an hour after the suspension determined the account should not have been removed. The coalition said millions took part in nearly 3,000 events in all 50 states and Washington, during an early-voting push before the 3 November midterms.

The explanation revises Meta's first account. Stone said on Saturday that unusually high rates of posting, sharing or commenting had triggered the automated systems, and called the removal "clearly" an error. "We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error", Stone said.

Bloomberg notes Stone's statement did not specify which Claude tool was involved, who was operating it, or what it had been doing in connection with the account. The International Business Times reports Democratic Senator Chris Murphy called for an investigation, arguing the incident exposed the "influence Meta holds over political discussion". The attribution is Meta's alone — neither Anthropic nor any independent review has confirmed it, and naming a tool does not establish who ran it.

items.headline: Reuters: AI industry expected to invest about $1 trillion next year as the Fed treats it as a price shock
bullets: Howard Schneider reports for Reuters that the AI industry is expected to invest about $1 trillion next year, roughly 3% of GDP, and that Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh called that investment a shock to prices and demand, saying central bankers "have got to recognize this as a shock" given their mandate for stable prices and full employment.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said higher rates could cool the economy "at the margins" and told Reuters "I'm not trying to stop growth", describing a wish to slow it enough to limit price pressure.

The Fed is expected to hold rates at 3.75%-4.00% at its 27-28 October meeting. Its 2% inflation goal has gone unmet for more than five years, while unemployment has stayed in a 4.0%-4.3% range for more than two years — so the cost of restraining AI-driven demand would fall on borrowers outside the AI build-out.

These are officials' characterisations of a shock, not a measured effect; the article does not report a quantified contribution of AI investment to inflation. reuters.com could not be opened from here, so the figures come from the Investing.com syndication of the Reuters wire.

items.headline: Disney agrees to offer jobs to at least 60 Character.AI employees at an estimated $60 million a year
bullets: TechCrunch, citing a legal filing spotted by Bloomberg, says Disney agreed to make employment offers to "at least 60" Character.AI employees — described as the majority of the workforce — "paying them an estimated $60 million in annual compensation", and that the "vast majority" of those offered jobs accepted.
The arrangement is a stalking horse bid, so another company could come forward with a higher offer. Character.AI had previously said Disney agreed to acquire some of its assets for $20 million.

The filing attributes the company's position, despite a "large and engaged user base", to high costs and "potential litigation-related liabilities and regulatory engagement". Character.AI was sued by the mother of a 14-year-old boy and faces government investigations over child safety.

TechCrunch did not access the filing itself, and the compensation figure is an estimate reported from it. The article links a report dated 13 October 2026 for the bankruptcy filing but does not state the exact filing date.

items.headline: World launches World ID for banks, with an AgentKit beta for delegating identity proofs to AI agents
bullets: PYMNTS reports World, the Sam Altman-backed identity project, announced World ID for banking and finance on Sunday 18 October, its first industry-specific product, aimed at helping businesses tell whether an AI agent is acting for a real person when it moves money or shops.

AgentKit, now in beta, lets a person delegate World ID Proofs to an AI agent, which can then present them to a website or service without revealing the person's information. The release describes this as distinguishing "an AI agent connected to a verified human" from "anonymous automated traffic".

The suite also includes World ID for Zoom, available through the Zoom App Marketplace for verifying participants in consequential video meetings, and the World ID app, available in 150-plus countries.

PYMNTS names no banks using the product and gives no pricing or number of verified humans. It cites PYMNTS Intelligence and Visa Acceptance Solutions research finding 56% of consumers would let an agent search and compare products but only 35% would give it access to saved payment credentials.
